Le trinitaire, *qui ne croit rien*, à rien, ne croit pas; il sait que le troisième rapport commun à *bien* et à *mal* est *hoc ceci*, ou *illud cela*, ou *istud nous* ; nous qui, dans la mobilité, ne sommes ni plus ni moins que ceci ou cela. Il sait aussi que les conséquences d'un principe ne sont, ni plus ni moins que ses bases.

Le trinitaire *sait* ou il doute; il s'arrête à ce dernier terme.

Il sait que les qualités contraires *bien* et *mal* emportent leur milieu *indifférent*, similairement à *chaud* et à *froid*, qui emportent tiède leur milieu : autant de *chaud*, autant de *froid*, autant de *tiède* ; autant de *bien*, autant d'*indifférent*, autant de *mal*. From experience, we have had and continue to have, by the hundreds and thousands, beliefs in these two principles considered as primitive. They are adopted under various illusory forms to which belief still attaches a *will*, and sets these wills against each other, <term>verbi gratia</term> <gloss>for example</gloss>: God-Devil. According to these beliefs, this will is absolute power, it is creative, it is sovereign law; there follows confusion in human laws which are copies of it, and confusion and war between believers. The trinitarian, *who believes nothing*, in nothing, does not believe; he knows that the third relationship common to *good* and *evil* is <term>hoc</term> <gloss>this</gloss>, or <term>illud</term> <gloss>that</gloss>, or <term>istud</term> <gloss>us</gloss>; we who, in mobility, are neither more nor less than this or that. He also knows that the consequences of a principle are neither more nor less than its bases.

The trinitarian *knows*, or he doubts; he stops at this last term.

He knows that the contrary qualities *good* and *evil* involve their *indifferent* <note>neutral or balanced</note> middle, similar to *hot* and *cold*, which involve lukewarm as their middle: as much as there is hot, there is as much cold, and as much lukewarm; as much as there is good, there is as much indifferent, and as much evil. The triple balance is exact; this is what must be recognized and experimented with.

Hinc igitur ego ad intellectum vulgarem (qui omnia considerat, prout oculis nunc se habent) Physicam meam atque Harmoniam eiusdem à Dei sede in circumferentia mundi seu eius summitate seu imaginata gradatim produxi, quamuis reuera Sapientibus exploratum atque explicatum sit, Deum esse vbique, & in Scripturis Sacris inuenimus, quod Deus impleat mundum sua præsentia & virtute, Atque ab essentia eius haud differt. Et ibidem inuenimus, quod spiritus disciplinæ sanctus impleat orbem terrarum, Atque hinc dictum est (vt antea) Iob 11. quod Sapientia Dei sit altissimis cælis altior, profundior sepulchro imo, longior terra mensura eius, & latior mari. Inde arguendo, eam esse in omnibus inter mundi peripheriam & eius centrum interuallis, atque iterum respectu sui extra omnia. Dicitur ergo Deus in cælo cælorum, quatenus in loco dignissimo, siue fit in terra siue in corporibus elementatis, siue in illis cælestibus, atque etiam in digniori & magis lucido ipsorum elementorum spiritu, igneo seu empyreo ob eius excellentiam dicto, qui vbique reperitur, quatenus Deus dicitur vbique, qui illud, videlicet Lucem primitus creatam, pro primario suo vestimento in hoc mundo eligit. Ad illud ergo vestimentum penetrauerunt oculi intellectuales ipsius Apostoli, quando dixit, se in cælum tertium fuisse raptum, vbi mirabilia & ineffabilia se vidisse narrat. Nam, vti diximus, vt cælum Empyreum seu Angelicum sumitur pro tertio cælo seu cælo cælorum, sic etiam si fit hoc cælum Dei folium, necesse est, vbi Deus fit, ibi etiam & cælu hoc: at Deus, vti dictum est, vbique essentialiter adest, Ergo & vbique est cælum illud, videlicet in Sole, quippe Dei tabernaculo, in nube densa, vtpote eius tigurio, in terra, cui datum est germinare Saluatorem, in Homine, vtpote Dei templo, & in qualibet Creatura, quatenus in Verbo est vita. Cælum igitur summum pro summa dignitate & puritate atque exaltatione sumitur. Sic Episcopum dignitate exaltatum dicimus, non dimensione quantitativa.

Dei autem demonstrationem & reuelationem, more mystico & non vulgari loquendo, à priori putamus potius esse à centro quam circumferentia. Nam nemo mentis sanæ dicet, circumferentiam esse suo centro, tempore & ordine priorem. Hinc ergo dictum est, Deum è tenebris ad mundi creationem apparuisse. Et Mercurius Trismegistus dixit, quod Monas generauerit Monadem & in seipsum reflexerit ardorem suum. Et sacræ Scripturæ agnoscunt, Deum in creatione apparuisse ex tenebris. & iterum, quod Tenebræ fuerint locus eius secretus. Atque hinc appellatur à Cabaliftis Deus latens, quatenus in se seu suo centro consideratur, atque etiam Aleph tenebrosum. Sed à suo puncto seu à se emittens radios suos circulariter hocque in infinitum, reducit aquas potenciales in actum: atque sic mundus est creatus, & hinc à Cabaliftis dicitur Aleph lucidus, & Deus patens, quæ est illa sapientia diuina, quæ effluxit atque emanauit à ſinu Patris ante omnia (vt in Ecclesiastico 1. reperitur) creata, iuxta illud Mercurij Trismegisti superius allegatum: Monas generat Monadem, &c. A terra ergo seu tenebrarum meditullio (quippe quæ Saluatorem germinare dicitur) tanquam à nobis manifestiori circuli mundani centro ad eiusdem peripheriam (imo vero & extra omnia) monochordum nostrum mundanum extendimus: ita & Aleph illud minus Cabaliftarum vnitatem importans in centro, hoc est, primo monochordi seu semidiametri extremo, posuimus, quod in monochordo notatur per C. Aleph vero magnum numeri millenarij character in eiusdem circumferentia multitudinem importante, iuxta illam Platonicorum enneadum dispositionem 999. vel literarum Iehouæ ordinationem, vbi Iod. 7. est centrum c. He prius est interuallum a. ad c. vt Vau explicatur per c. naturam Solis internam arguens. & vltimum He postremum Dei in multitudinem progressum, quo iterum redit ad se videl. ad Iod, à quo est prius effluxum. Atque hinc hæ literæ obseruantur à Cabaliftis esse solummodo inter omnes alias literas Hebraicas sphæricæ & rotundæ. Videmus ergo quod inter Iod & Vau, videlicet per He seu spiritum purum consonantia Diapason spiritualis reperitur, vtpote immediate à Iod è tenebris ad mundi creationem emanans, vnde Lux & cælum Empyreum primo die sunt creata, & cælum æthereum secundo, mouente Spiritu Domini Vau siue Mettatron super aquas vice Solis. Deinde inter Vau ad Iod iterum, videl. per spacium He seu spiritum groſſum siue elementarem altera consonantia Diapason videl. illa materialis constituitur: & per hunc nexum harmonicum materialia à circumferentia seu Deo transeunt in spiritualia, & illa tandem in ipsum Deum, qui est centrum, vnde Iod, He & Vau omnia monochordo mundana implet. Sed hæc omnia dices fortaſſis mystica & Cabalistica: procedamus ergo via magis aperta & oculis tuis perspicua. Vides monochordi chordam æqualiter tensam non esse nisi vnicam, & vnicum certum & immobilem sonum edere pulsatam: at si directe in medietate prematur, videlicet m.c. dabit vtraque portio æqualis, videlicet n. C. & c. C. sonos eosdem & æquales, hoc est, eiusdem toni, & tamen portio, chordæ c. C. comparata ad totam chordam C. n. dabit percussa primam consonantiam Diapason, atque identidem portio c. n. percussa cum tota, secundam, proportionem duplam in omnibus priorisimile, præterquam quod hæc fit in multitudine magis immerſa, vtpote à fonte c. magis dilatata. Hinc ergo in hoc experimento oculari habemus vnum ante aliqua dimenſionem, videl. chordam per se solam & in se totam consideramus: a. c. ad n. habemus etiam & 2. videl. duas chordæ portiones, duplicem consonantiam Diapason cum toto seu vnitate chordæ ſonantes. From this, therefore, I have produced my Physics and the Harmony of the same for the vulgar intellect (which considers all things as they now present themselves to the eyes) gradually from the seat of God in the circumference of the world or its summit or imagined [place], although in truth it has been explored and explained by the Wise that God is everywhere, and in the Holy Scriptures we find that God fills the world with His presence and power. And He does not differ from His essence. And in the same place we find that the holy spirit of discipline fills the orb of the earth, and hence it was said (as before) in Job 11 that the Wisdom of God is higher than the highest heavens, deeper than the grave, longer in measure than the earth, and broader than the sea. From that, arguing that it is in all intervals between the periphery of the world and its center, and again, with respect to Himself, outside all things. God is therefore said to be in the heaven of heavens, insofar as it is in the most worthy place, whether it be on earth or in elemental bodies, or in those celestial ones, and also in the more worthy and more lucid spirit of the elements themselves, called igneous or empyrean on account of its excellence, which is found everywhere, insofar as God is said to be everywhere, who chooses that, namely the Light created at first, for His primary garment in this world. To that garment, therefore, the intellectual eyes of the Apostle himself penetrated, when he said that he had been rapt into the third heaven, where he narrates that he saw wonders and ineffable things. For, as we have said, as the Empyrean or Angelic heaven is taken for the third heaven or the heaven of heavens, so also if this heaven is the leaf of God, it is necessary that where God is, there also is this heaven: but God, as has been said, is present everywhere essentially, therefore that heaven is also everywhere, namely in the Sun, indeed the tabernacle of God, in the dense cloud, as His hut, on earth, which was given to germinate the Savior, in Man, as the temple of God, and in any Creature, insofar as life is in the Word. The highest heaven is therefore taken for the highest dignity and purity and exaltation. Thus we call a Bishop exalted in dignity, not by quantitative dimension.

However, we think the demonstration and revelation of God, speaking in a mystical and not a vulgar way, <term>a priori</term> is rather from the center than the circumference. For no one of sound mind will say that the circumference is prior to its center in time and order. Hence, therefore, it was said that God appeared from darkness to the creation of the world. And Mercurius Trismegistus said that the Monad generated a Monad and reflected its heat into itself. And the Holy Scriptures recognize that God appeared in creation from darkness. And again, that Darkness was His secret place. And hence God is called by the Cabalists the hidden God, insofar as He is considered in Himself or His center, and also the dark <term>Aleph</term> <gloss>first Hebrew letter</gloss>. But from His point or from Himself emitting His rays circularly and this into infinity, He reduces the potential waters into act: and thus the world is created, and hence He is called by the Cabalists the luminous <term>Aleph</term>, and the manifest God, which is that divine wisdom which flowed and emanated from the bosom of the Father before all things (as is found in Ecclesiasticus 1) created, according to that of Mercurius Trismegistus cited above: The Monad generates a Monad, etc. From the earth therefore or the center of darkness (inasmuch as it is said to germinate the Savior) as if from the center of the mundane circle more manifest to us, we extend our mundane monochord to its periphery (indeed even outside all things): thus we have placed that lesser <term>Aleph</term> of the Cabalists, importing unity in the center, that is, the first extreme of the monochord or semi-diameter, which is noted in the monochord by C. But the great <term>Aleph</term>, the character of the thousandth number, [importing] multitude in the same circumference, according to that disposition of the Platonic enneads 999, or the ordination of the letters of <term>Iehoua</term> <gloss>Jehovah</gloss>, where <term>Iod</term> is the center c., <term>He</term> prior is the interval a. to c., as <term>Vau</term> is explained through the internal nature of the Sun arguing <term>c.</term> And the last <term>He</term> [is] the last progress of God into the multitude, by which He returns again to Himself, namely to <term>Iod</term>, from which He first flowed. And hence these letters are observed by the Cabalists to be, among all other Hebrew letters, alone spherical and round. We see therefore that between <term>Iod</term> and <term>Vau</term>, namely through <term>He</term> or pure spirit, the spiritual <term>diapason</term> consonance is found, as emanating immediately from <term>Iod</term> from darkness to the creation of the world, whence Light and the Empyrean heaven are created on the first day, and the ethereal heaven on the second, with the Spirit of the Lord <term>Vau</term> or <term>Metatron</term> moving over the waters in place of the Sun. Then between <term>Vau</term> to <term>Iod</term> again, namely through the space <term>He</term> or gross or elemental spirit, another <term>diapason</term> consonance is constituted, namely that material one: and through this harmonic link, material things pass from the circumference or God into spiritual things, and those at last into God Himself, who is the center, whence <term>Iod</term>, <term>He</term> and <term>Vau</term> fill all things of the mundane monochord. But you will perhaps say all these are mystical and Cabalistic: let us proceed therefore by a way more open and clear to your eyes. You see the string of the monochord equally stretched is but a single one, and when struck it emits a single certain and immobile sound: but if it is pressed directly in the middle, namely m.c., each equal portion will give, namely n. C. and c. C., the same and equal sounds, that is, of the same tone, and yet the portion of the string c. C. compared to the whole string C. n. will give when struck the first <term>diapason</term> consonance, and likewise the portion c. n. struck with the whole, the second, the duple proportion in all things similar to the prior, except that this happens more immersed in the multitude, as if more dilated from the source c. We see Anaximander here affirming a double infinity: an infinite extension, the principle of the coexistence of an infinity of simultaneous worlds; and an infinite eternity, the principle of the periodic generations and destructions of an infinity of successive worlds.

In different terms, the same ideas are attributed to Anaximander by the work titled *Philosophumena* or *Refutatio omnium hæresium* <gloss>Refutation of all Heresies</gloss>, which was long attributed to Origen and which is now restored to Saint Hippolytus. Here, in fact, is what this work reports of the teaching of Anaximander <note>1</note>:

> "He says that the principle of beings is a certain nature of the infinite; from this nature are born the heavens and the worlds they contain. It is eternal and never grows old, this nature which encompasses all worlds."

To this, Saint Hippolytus adds this important sentence: "Anaximander says that time is [formed] as the delimited sum of the generation, existence, and destruction [of a world] (<term>λέγει δὲ χρόνον ὡς ὡρισμένης τῆς γενέσεως καὶ τῆς οὐσίας καὶ τῆς φθορᾶς</term>)." For the first time, we glimpse here the idea that true time, that perfect duration, is the well-determined duration that flows from the birth to the death of one of the successive worlds, and that it is the period according to which the Universe reproduces itself. Soon, Archytas of Tarentum will tell us what importance this thought took in the Pythagorean theory of time.

Like Anaximander, Anaximenes certainly admitted the successive existence of an infinity of worlds whose births and deaths were regulated by a well-determined period of time. Simplicius affirms this for us in these very terms. There are philosophers, he says <note>2</note>, who believe that "a world always exists; but it is not the same world that always exists; what exists is sometimes one world, sometimes another, whose generation occurs according to certain periods of time (<term>γινόμενον κατά τινας χρόνων περιόδους</term>). This is what Anaximenes, Heraclitus, Diogenes, and, later, the Stoics thought."

From the moment that, in the infinite succession of worlds, each world has a limited duration—the same for all—the knowledge of this duration appears to man as one of the most captivating objects that can hold his curiosity. He must have attempted early on to determine this duration and to compare the period of the...

Avant qu'une substance puisse croître ou décroître, avant que les qualités dont elle est douée puissent éprouver quelque variation, il faut qu'elle soit engendrée. Or, comment une substance pourrait-elle être engendrée, comment, dans une portion déterminée de la matière première, une forme, jusqu'alors en puissance, passerait-elle à l'existence actuelle, s'il ne survenait quelque changement dans les circonstances où cette portion de matière se trouve placée? Et comment ces circonstances changeraient-elles, si quelque corps étranger ne s'approchait ou ne s'éloignait de celui qui contient cette matière première? Ainsi, au point de départ de toute génération, nous trouvons quelque mouvement local.

« Puis donc que la génération ne peut être le premier des mouvements, ... il est évident qu'aucun des mouvements qui la suivent ne peut être le premier; par mouvements qui la suivent, j'entends la dilatation, l'altération, la contraction et la corruption, car elles sont toutes postérieures à la génération ; en sorte que, si la génération n'est pas antérieure au mouvement local, aucune des autres transformations ne saurait, d'aucune manière, précéder ce mouvement. »

Toute génération donc, toute variation de densité, toute altération, toute destruction serait impossible si quelque mouvement local n'avait approché ou éloigné le corps dont le déplacement détermine tous ces changements. Since local movement is the only one which can be eternal, it is necessarily, in time, before any other movement. It must be, moreover, that local movement precedes all other movements, for it is from it that these derive all their primary origin.

Before a substance can grow or diminish, before the qualities with which it is endowed can experience some variation, it must be generated. Now, how could a substance be generated, how, in a determined portion of prime matter, would a form, until then in potentiality, pass to current existence, if some change did not occur in the circumstances where this portion of matter is placed? And how would these circumstances change, if some foreign body did not approach or move away from the one that contains this prime matter? Thus, at the starting point of all generation, we find some local movement.

"Since, therefore, generation cannot be the first of movements, ... it is evident that none of the movements which follow it can be the first; by movements which follow it, I mean dilation, alteration, contraction, and corruption, for they are all posterior to generation; so that, if generation is not prior to local movement, none of the other transformations could, in any way, precede this movement."

Every generation, therefore, every variation of density, every alteration, every destruction would be impossible if some local movement had not approached or moved away the body whose displacement determines all these changes. Likewise, the generations, the variations of size and quality, the destructions which occur within nature could not last indefinitely if perpetual local movements did not periodically displace the immutable and eternal bodies whose approach or distancing determines these transformations.

"It has been demonstrated," says Aristotle <note>1</note>, "that there exists a perpetual local movement; this being established, it results necessarily that generation..."

[it] stands that the creature acts by itself, that is, by some free choice or its own will, which is absolutely divided and clearly distinguished from the immediate act of the Divinity. To these people, who are inconsistent with themselves, I respond according to the rules or canons established in the Divinity: that the divine essence is indivisible. Therefore, it is evident that God is not accustomed to impart any essential act, such as the soul, life, and the functions depending thereon, to any of the creatures, which could be discontinued or separated from His nature, according to the axiom: what God has given, He never withdraws. And for this reason, Christ, who is the eternal spirit of wisdom, is said to fill all things. Indeed (the worldly wise man of this age will reply), who attempts to distract men from the simple truth with vain distinctions: this presence of divinity is in every thing virtually and not essentially or substantially. To him I say: I would gladly like to know (holding such academic distinctions for nothing), for Saint Paul commands Timothy: if anyone, he says, teaches a different doctrine and does not approach the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ and the doctrine of the fear of God, he is one who is puffed up, knowing nothing, but is obsessed with disputes and arguments about words, from which come envy, contention, slander, and evil suspicion. And the friction of men whose mind is corrupted, and who are destitute of the truth and think that godliness is a means of gain. From such withdraw yourself. I would gladly (I say) like to know whether the virtue of God is not His essence, or whether one can be distinguished or separated from the other? If, however, he answers that the divine virtue is not the essence, but an accident, it must be believed for certain that such an answer is erroneous. Since it is manifest, and known even to the Jews and gentiles themselves, that God is free from every accident, since He is the most essential essence of all, existing in Himself and by Himself, not subject to any accident. Furthermore, where His essential act is present, there also is His virtue; and where His virtue is, whose role it is to give life to all things; indeed, if it were otherwise, the Word of God or the divine act, whose role it is to render all things agile and mobile, would seem to be nothing, except a mere accident; indeed, an accident separated from the divine essence. The immortality of the root itself argues how absurd this would be. For David, in the text cited above, has: by the spirit of the heavens, etc. I believe there is no one so lacking in mind as to hold this virtue for an accident. It follows, therefore, that divine virtue is the same as the divine essence, and consequently in God Himself and from God, that is, never separated from the divine spirit. But why say more? Since we have this expressly confirmed by the scriptures: The spirit (says
<margin>1.7.25.26.</margin>
Solomon) is a vapor of the virtue of God, and a sincere flow from the glory of the Almighty, and a splendor from the eternal light, etc. What? Shall we call this virtue or splendor proceeding from the eternal light an accident, when it is the holy spirit of wisdom, as the wise man confesses? Hence
<margin>Col. 1.16; John 1.</margin>
also Saint Paul in the place cited before: In Him all things were created in heaven and on earth, both visible and invisible; all things were created in Him and through Him, and in Him they stand, etc. From which it is clear that outside of Him and the spirit, there is nothing. And John: In the Word was life, etc. And consequently it is clear that the creature is continued and annexed to the divinity through the bond of this divine nature, that is, through one and the same spirit of Life that is in it; without which nexus, union, or relation to one another, it is impossible for the creature to exist for a moment of time. Hence, therefore, the Royal Psalmist says: All creatures look to
<margin>Ps. 104.24, etc.</margin>
You, that You may give them food in due season. When You give it to them, they gather it; when You open Your hand, they are filled with good. When You hide Your face, they are troubled; when You take away their spirit, they expire; when You send forth Your spirit, they are recreated with good, etc. From which it may be seen that it is the immediate act of this wisdom that makes the creature live and exist, and that it is He who works all things. For the scriptures testify that God gives life to all things, and that in Him we live, move, and have our being, and not only we, but also every flesh in general, as we gather from this very text. And also from this testimony of Job: If God should set His heart upon man,
<margin>Job 34.14.</margin>
and gather to Himself his spirit or his breath, all flesh would perish together, and man would return to dust, etc. Behold, therefore, the Corner-Stone upon which all flesh is built, and without which it is reduced to nothing. Furthermore, the Prophet says: God gives breath to the people who are upon the earth, and spirit to those who walk upon it, etc. How (I ask you) is it possible that this spirit of life is present in and with all things, and therefore essentially in every thing, and yet would cease and rest from its immediate action, when it is in itself the swiftest of all things and most agile and mobile, as we are taught by Solomon?
<margin>Wis. 7.</margin>

A ces physiciens, Guillaume de Conches oppose les autorités du Timée, de Johannitius, de Macrobe ; toutes proclament que l'élément est le sujet qu'affectent les qualités, et non pas ces qualités mêmes.

Il va sans dire que Guillaume n'admet, pour constituer les corps, rien d'autre que les quatre éléments ; de la cinquième essence péripatéticienne, il ne parle même pas. « Le feu remplit l'espace qui s'étend au-dessus de la Lune¹ ; c'est ce même feu qu'on nomme éther. L'ornement de ce corps qui se trouve au-dessus de la Lune est constitué par les étoiles, tant fixes qu'errantes. »

Les étoiles qui, comme les cieux eux-mêmes, sont formées par l'élément igné, sont-elles en mouvement ? Telle est la première question proprement astronomique qu'examine Guillaume de Conches² : « Les uns prétendent qu'elles ne se meuvent pas, mais qu'elles sont entraînées d'Orient en Occident par le firmament, au sein duquel elles sont fixées. D'autres disent que elles se meuvent d'un mouvement propre, car elles sont de nature ignée, et rien ne saurait se soutenir sans mouvement au sein de l'éther ou du fluide céleste ; mais ils pensent qu'elles se meuvent sur place, en tournant sur elles-mêmes. Les troisièmes assurent qu'elles se meuvent en passant d'un lieu à un autre, mais que nos yeux ne peuvent aucunement percevoir leur mouvement ; elles emploient, en effet, un tel laps de temps à parcourir leurs divers cercles que la vie humaine, qui est courte, ne suffit pas à saisir même une brève portion de cette si lente circulation ».

of Constantine, nor those of any physicist; their pride is such that they would be indignant to learn anything at all from another; they have the arrogance to imagine what they do not know, in order to appear to be saying something; these people say that the elements are nothing other than the qualities of the bodies that are seen, namely: dry, cold, moist, hot."

To these physicists, William of Conches opposes the authorities of the *Timaeus*, of Johannitius, and of Macrobius; all proclaim that the element is the subject that the qualities affect, and not these qualities themselves.

It goes without saying that William admits, to constitute bodies, nothing other than the four elements; of the Peripatetic fifth essence, he does not even speak. "Fire fills the space that extends above the Moon; it is this same fire that is named ether. The ornament of this body that is found above the Moon is constituted by the stars, both fixed and wandering."

Are the stars, which like the heavens themselves are formed by the igneous element, in movement? Such is the first properly astronomical question that William of Conches examines: "Some claim that they do not move, but that they are carried from East to West by the firmament, in the midst of which they are fixed. Others say that they move with their own movement, for they are of an igneous nature, and nothing could sustain itself without movement in the midst of the ether or the celestial fluid; but they think that they move in place, by turning upon themselves. The third party assures that they move by passing from one place to another, but that our eyes cannot perceive their movement at all; they employ, in effect, such a lapse of time to traverse their various circles that human life, which is short, does not suffice to grasp even a brief portion of this so slow circulation."

This allusion to the slow movement of the fixed stars is textually borrowed from Macrobius; but the following belongs properly to William: "We share this opinion that the stars move by passing from one place to another; but that their movement is not perceptible, we propose another reason for it, which..."

<summary>William of Conches refutes the notion that elements are merely visible qualities, identifying them instead as underlying subjects, and discusses the movement of fixed stars within the ethereal realm.</summary>

translation.data: When they had come to the king, they were kindly received by him. Staying for twelve days with the king, he inquired of them about things he had disposed of in his heart, and especially about two things: namely, the knowledge of God and the government of the kingdom. When they had instructed him in the administration of the kingdom, they then disputed more fully about worshipping the one God, [emphasizing] that no creature is God. Hence it is that wherever a mention of the Trinity occurred to them, they either passed over it in silence or translated it enigmatically, lest they appear to have taught that three gods should be worshipped. Similarly, mentioning the incarnation of the Word, as in Isaiah, when they had said, "A child is born to us," and he had added his names, for those six names they translated "Angel of Great Counsel," lest they appear to have taught that a man was made God. Then they showed the king the scroll they had, and he could not stop admiring the thinness of the pages and the pagination, which could not be comprehended by the eyes, and how the golden letters appeared so legible against the whiteness of the pages. They were introduced into the king's house by the sea, which was secret for the deliberation of business, and individual cells were given to them for whatever seemed opportune to them for translating. And, observing the rite of their purifications and prayers each day, they would wash themselves in the sea for the Law. Furthermore, they translated until the ninth hour, then they passed to food and rest, and they completed the work in seventy-one days. Augustine says that it was miraculously done that one and the same edition was found without difference, and that they translated the Law, the Psalms, and the Prophets in so many days. Jerome, however, seems to want to say that the translators conferred on the Sabbath of six days, forging one from them all. The work being completed, Demetrius gathered all the Jews who were in Alexandria and those more skilled from the province, and their translation was read before everyone and approved. Furthermore, it was brought to the king and replicated before him. When the interpreters asked of the king that authority be given so that it might remain immovable, he praised that he would do this if at last they collected those things so chastely that what was once judged would not be forced to be irritated. And he sent them back honored with gifts. He also sent gifts to Eleazar. To the temple, however, he sent a vessel adorned with inappreciable gems, whose thickness was half a cubit, yet the workmanship exceeded the material. This Ptolemy composed canons of the stars and wrote many books. He was also very skilled and most learned in the quadrivium. He made a description of the orb of the earth and found the number of stadia of the earth and the circles of the earth with wonderful subtlety and ingenuity. At that time, the Carthaginians defeated the Romans in a naval battle, having put Metellus to flight, and captured Marcus Regulus with five hundred noble Romans and killed three hundred thousand of them. Finally, the Carthaginians sent Regulus to Rome so that he might negotiate about peace and the exchange of captives between them and the Romans. Coming to Rome, he persuaded the Senate not to make peace, nor to return so many thousands of Carthaginian captives for the sake of himself or a few captured Romans. Liber Secundus

Arguitur si anima est in qualibet parte essentia. ergo per virtutem etiam in animalibus presentia. que potentia sequitur per essentia. et tunc est vera potentia. essentia sibi proportionatur. et tunc non est vera potentia. essentia sibi proportionatur. et tunc non est vera potentia. et patitur ad partes corporis et non ad totum corpus sibi proportionatur. et tunc non est vera potentia sequitur essentia. Alio modo accipit essentia animae sequitur essentia. et hoc per alii sic dicunt. utique tota essentia ibi est tota potentia in radice et non in actu.

Arguitur si anima est in qualibet parte corporis tunc sequeretur quod idem esset movens et motum simul. et idem moveret et quiesceret. et una manus moveri potest alia quiescere. et anima movere sursum et ad totum corpus. et idem moveret contrariis motibus quod est inconveniens. Domine dupliciter. Primo quod non proprie moveat alia parte corporis mota. quod quis anima moveret moto toto corpore non est movere ad motione partis. quia anima non est proprie parte. Secundo concessio quia anima est ad motione partis. tunc dicit domine quod non est inconveniens unum et idem passum moveri et quiescere et moveri contrariis motibus et hoc si motu non est perfecte una et continua. Exempli extra posita. ut aliqui contingit existentes in navi quiescere cum se et in moveri per motus navis. Ita contingit aliqui existente in navi moveri contrariis motibus quod est cum navi descendere et per motum proprie ascendere contra motum navis. Sile domine ex anima existente in parte corporis et qua partes animalis sunt perfecte continue sic una pars potest moveri alia quiescere. et una pars potest moveri sursum alia vero vorsum.

Arguitur anima rationalis est indivisibilis vel indivisibilis quod vel est corpore extensiva vel non extensa. si est corpore extensive sic est divisibilis. si non extensa sic est indivisibilis. Domine quod duplex extensio. quod est extensio quantitativa sicut albedo extendit in pariete. et sic anima non est extensa in corpore quod tunc divideret ad divisionem corporis. Alia est extensio essentialiter informat qualibet parte animae et non oportet quod sit extensum dividatur ad divisionem corporis divisi.

Quod autem quibus.
Dicenter solvit prima questione prius motam quod fuit. An vegetativum. sensitivum. et intellectivum sint partes animae diverse vel una anima. Domine quod ista dicta est vegetativum. sensitivum. intellectivum et motuum duplex. Uno put invenitur in animalibus segregatim. et sic sunt diverse animae. Ad sic probat Aristoteles quod quando inveniuntur in

<column-break/>

universis tunc penes istas animas sumit differentia animalium. sed differentia sumitur ex forma substantiali. ergo in diversis animas que tunc possibile esset diversitas animas que inveniuntur in uno eodem. et sic non significat diversitas animas. quod tunc possibile esset diversitas animas. Unum per homine non sunt diverse animae. quia tunc in uno homine sint vegetativum. sensitivum. intellectivum et motuum.

Querit utrum anima vegetativa. sensitiva. in intellectiva sit una anima vel plures animae. Domine quod ista tria in uno numero sunt una anima numero sicut in homine. et hoc per tribus rationibus ducentibus ad impossibile et una ratione omnium. Prima ratio stat in hoc. si plures formae substantiales essent in uno subiecto et materia sequeretur quod unum ens in numero esset plura entia substantialia. sic sequela est impossibilis. quod implicat contradictionem. Sequela tunc perque forma substantialis aliquid est simpliciter ens cum ipsa dat simpliciter esse. Si anima est forma substantialis. quia sunt plures animae in uno homine sunt plura entia substantialia. Secunda ratio sumitur ex modo predicandi. et stat in hoc. si anima sensitiva et intellectiva diverse sint animae tunc ista propositio homo est animal vel esset falsa vel per accidens. quod utrumque est contra intentionem Aristotelis. Secundo posterio. Sequela perque quod predicatio quod fit per diversas formas vel est falsa si formae non sunt subordinate. ut album est dulce. ibi predicatur diverse formae non subordinate. vel si formae sunt subordinate et predicatio per accidens. ut lupicies est colorata. lupicies est in subiecto primo. Siter quod ista propositio homo est animal et diversis formis. et forma rationali et sensitiva non est esse in primo modo per se. Tercia ratio stat in hoc. quod si anima vegetativa. sensitiva. et intellectiva essent diversae animae in uno homine sequeretur quod operationes factas ab alia anima. si hoc est falsum. ergo sunt una anima. Maior patet. quia quando sunt simpliciter diversa unum non impedit alterum. Minor quod si operatio unum animae fit multum intellectiva tunc impedit operatio sensitiva. contingit etiam et intellectiva virtutem et multum intenta imaginatione impediri virtutem intellectivam. contingit etiam et intellectiva impediri operationes sensitivas. Ratio omnium stat in hoc. sic et hoc numerum altior et supior ad numerum inferiorem. ita est haec anima dignior ad minus digna. sed si per hoc numerum includit inferiorem. quod supior anima includit inferiorem. sic intellectiva includit sensitivam et sensitiva vegetativam. Maior patet. quia species rerum sumitur ex animabus. sicut ergo species rerum se habent ut numeri ita et animae. et hoc quod dicit infra.

Book Two

It is argued: if the soul is in every part by essence, then it is also present by power in animals, since power follows essence. And then it is a true power, the essence is proportioned to itself, and then it is not a true power. It suffers toward the parts of the body and not to the whole body proportioned to itself, and then it is not a true power that follows essence. In another way, one accepts the essence of the soul as following essence. And others say it thus: certainly the whole essence is there, the whole power is in the root and not in act.

It is argued: if the soul is in every part of the body, then it would follow that the same thing would be moving and moved at the same time, and the same thing would move and rest. And one hand can be moved while the other rests, and the soul can move upward and toward the whole body, and the same thing would move with contrary motions, which is inconvenient. I say this is answered in two ways. First, that it does not properly move while another part of the body is moved; that the soul would move with the whole body being moved is not moving according to the motion of a part, because the soul is not properly a part. Second, conceding that the soul is according to the motion of a part, then I say that it is not inconvenient for one and the same patient to be moved and to rest and to be moved with contrary motions, provided the motion is not perfectly one and continuous. Examples are provided externally, as happens to some existing in a ship resting with it and being moved through the motion of the ship. So it happens to someone existing in a ship to be moved by contrary motions, which is to descend with the ship and by one's own motion to ascend against the motion of the ship. Similarly, I say that from the soul existing in a part of the body, and since the parts of the animal are perfectly continuous, thus one part can be moved and the other rest, and one part can be moved upward and the other downward.

It is argued: the rational soul is indivisible, or it is indivisible, either it is extensive in the body or not extensive. If it is bodily extensive, then it is divisible; if not extensive, then it is indivisible. I say there is a twofold extension. One is quantitative extension, just as whiteness extends in a wall, and thus the soul is not extended in the body, for then it would be divided according to the division of the body. The other is essential extension; it informs every part of the soul, and it is not necessary that what is extended be divided according to the division of the divided body.

As to which [soul].
The speaker solves the first question raised earlier, which was: whether the vegetative, sensitive, and intellective are diverse parts of the soul or one soul. I say that this is said: the vegetative, sensitive, intellective, and the movement are twofold. One way, as they are found in animals separately, and thus they are diverse souls. And thus Aristotle proves that when they are found in 

<column-break/>

all, then the difference of animals is taken from these souls, but the difference is taken from the substantial form. Therefore, there are diverse souls, which would then make possible the diversity of souls that are found in one and the same. And thus, it does not signify a diversity of souls, for then a diversity of souls would be possible. In a human, there are not diverse souls, because then in one human there would be a vegetative, sensitive, intellective, and movement.

He asks whether the vegetative, sensitive, and intellective soul is one soul or several souls. I say that these three in one number are one soul in number, as in a human, and this is by three reasons leading to the impossible and one reason of all. The first reason stands in this: if several substantial forms were in one subject and matter, it would follow that one being in number would be several substantial beings. Such a consequence is impossible, for it implies a contradiction. The consequence then is that through a substantial form something is simply a being, since it gives simple being. If the soul is a substantial form, because there are several souls in one human, there are several substantial beings. The second reason is taken from the mode of predicating, and it stands in this: if the sensitive and intellective souls were diverse souls, then this proposition "a human is an animal" would either be false or accidental, both of which are against the intention of Aristotle. Second, posteriorly. The consequence follows that the predication made through diverse forms is either false if the forms are not subordinate, as "the white is sweet"—there, diverse forms not subordinate are predicated—or if the forms are subordinate, the predication is accidental, as "a fox is colored," the fox is in the subject primarily. I say that this proposition "a human is an animal" and [with] diverse forms, the rational and sensitive form, is not to be in the first mode per se. The third reason stands in this: that if the vegetative, sensitive, and intellective souls were diverse souls in one human, it would follow that operations done by one soul [would not be hindered by another]. If this is false, then they are one soul. The major is clear, because when they are simply diverse, one does not impede the other. The minor is that if the operation of one soul is done, much intellective, then it impedes the sensitive operation; it happens also that the intellective [impedes] the power, and with much intent imagination, the intellective power is impeded. It happens also that the intellective impedes sensitive operations. The reason of all stands in this: as this number is higher and superior to the lower number, so this soul is more worthy to the less worthy. But if by this the number includes the lower, because the superior soul includes the inferior, thus the intellective includes the sensitive, and the sensitive the vegetative. The major is clear, because the species of things are taken from souls; as therefore the species of things relate as numbers, so also the souls, and this is what he says below.

<summary>This page explores the unity of the soul, arguing that the vegetative, sensitive, and intellective powers in a human constitute a single substantial form rather than multiple distinct souls.</summary>

Sentiri sine sensu: si sensus est quaedam ratio, et proportio et potentia illius magnitudinis. Deinde cum dicit, manifestum est ex his praemissis concludit solum quadam modo quod posset quaeri. Et manifestum est ex praedictis propter quod excellentia sensibilium corrumpat organa sensuum, et in organis sentiendi ad hoc quod sentiat est quaedam ratio, et proportio, ut dictum est. Si ergo motus sensibilis fuerit fortior, hoc organum natum est pati: solvit proportio et corrumpit sensum, et consistit in quadam proportione organi, ut dictum est. Et sicut sicut cum aliquis forte percutit cordas, solvit symphonia et tonus in qua proportione consistit. Manifesta est etiam ex praedictis ratio alterius quaestionis propter quod plantae non sentiunt: cum in habeat quadam proportionem ad quaedam sensibilia, scilicet ad tangibilia. Manifestum est enim quod calefacit et infrigidat. Et igitur quaerendo non requirit ad sentiendum, non enim habet medietatem complexionis inter tangibilia quod nullus sensus esse potest. Et non habet se huiusmodi principium quod recipit species sine materia sensu: sed accidit eis pati cum materia, et est materiale transmutatione. Deinde cum dicit dubitabit aut aliquis, movet quadam modo circa passione a sensibilibus, quae ei dixerat quod plantae patiuntur a sensibilibus. Primo movet dubium utrum ab aliis sensibilibus aliquid possit pati quod non habet sensum, puta ab odore: quod non habet olfactum, a colore quod non habet visum, a sono quod non habet auditum, secundo ibi. Simul autem inducit duas rationes ad ostendendum quod non, quia prima talis est, quod proprium olfactibilis est facere relfatu: odor autem facit olfactibile, ergo si aliquid facit olfactum, et quod facit olfatum sive faceret et littera odor facit: propria igitur actio odoris in quo sequitur quod suscipies actione odoris in quantum odor: habet sensum olfactus quod ergo non habet sensum olfactus non potest pati ab odore, et eadem ratio videtur de aliis et non quorumcumque posse pati a sensibilibus: sed solum habentium sensum. Secundam rationem ponit, ibi. Manifestum est autem quod corpus primum ad concludendum, manifestum est per experimentum: quod lumen et tenebra et odor et sonum nullus effectus facit in corpora insensibilia: nisi

forte per accidens: inquantum corpora bruta huiusmodi qualitates aliquando agunt: sicut aer quando est tonitruum scindit lignum, lignum enim patitur non a sono per se loquendo: sed ab aere moto. Tertio ibi. Sed tangentia, ostendit aliter esse de qualitatibus tangentibus, et dicit quod tangibilia et humores, id est, pores faciunt quaedam effectum in sensibilibus, sed bene intelligendum est de saporibus: non inquantum tangibile, et quantum tactum. Si ei corpora insensibilia non paterent a qualitatibus sensibilibus non esset ponere a quo paterent et alterarent corpora inanimata, nam tangibilia sunt qualitates active et passive elementorum quas accidit universaliter alteratio in corporibus. Quarto ibi, ergo ne illa, ostendit etiam quod alia tangibilia sensibilia agunt in quaedam res inanimatas: sed non omnes dicit ergo ne illa, ostendit alia faciant aliquem effectum et olfatu in res inanimatas, quod dicit: sed tamen non omne corpus passivum est ab odore et sono: sicut omne corpus passivum est a calore et frigore. Sed ab istis sensibilibus pati possunt sola corpora indeterminata et quae non manent, ut aer et aqua quae sunt humida et non bene determinabilia termino proprio, et quod aer possit pati ab odore manifestum est quia aer fetet sicut aliquid patens ab odore, alia littera habet feret: quia scilicet media et aliis sensibilibus feret species ad sensum, sed huiusmodi diversitatis est: quia alitates tangibiles sunt causae aliorum sensibilium, et ideo habent plus de virtute activa: et possunt agere in quecumque corpora: sed alia sensibilia quae habent minus de virtute activa: non possunt agere nisi in corpora valde passibilia, et sic etiam ratio est de luce corporum caelestium quae alterant inferiora corpora. Qui toti ibi, quod est igitur, solvit rationem et positam: dicens: quia si aliquid patitur ab odore quod non odorat: quid est odorare nisi pati aliquid ab odore, et respondet quod odorare est sic pati ab odore et sentiat odore, et erat non sic patitur ut sentiat quia non habet potentiam sensitivam: sed sic patitur ut sit sensibilis inquantum est medium in sensu.

Then, when he says <note>a red paragraph mark follows</note> "it is manifest from these premises," he concludes only in a certain way what could be asked. And it is manifest from the aforesaid why the excellence of the sensibles corrupts the organs of the senses, and that in the organs of sensing there is, for the purpose of sensing, a certain ratio and proportion, as was said. If, therefore, the motion of the sensible were stronger, this organ is born to suffer, it dissolves the proportion and corrupts the sense, and it consists in a certain proportion of the organ, as was said. And just as when someone strikes the strings forcefully, it dissolves the symphony and the tone in which the proportion consists. The reason for another question is also manifest from the aforesaid, why plants do not sense, since they have a certain proportion to certain sensibles, namely to tangibles. For it is manifest that it heats and cools. And therefore, in seeking, it does not require for sensing, for it does not have the mean of complexion between tangibles, without which no sense can exist. And it does not have that kind of principle that receives species without matter in the sense, but it happens to them to suffer with matter, and it is material through transmutation.

Then, when he says "some will doubt," he moves in a certain way regarding passion from the sensibles, which he had told it that plants suffer from the sensibles. First, he moves the doubt whether anything can suffer from other sensibles that does not have a sense, for example from an odor, that which does not have smell; from a color, that which does not have sight; from a sound, that which does not have hearing. Second, at the point "simultaneously, however," he induces two reasons to show that it does not. Because the first is such, that it is proper to the odorous to cause olfaction; odor, however, makes the odorous, therefore if anything makes olfaction, and that which makes olfaction or would make, the odor makes; the proper action of odor is therefore that in which it follows that you will receive the action of odor insofar as it is odor; therefore it has the sense of smell; what therefore does not have the sense of smell cannot suffer from odor, and the same reason seems to hold for others, and that not just anything can suffer from sensibles, but only those having a sense.

He poses the second reason there: "It is manifest, however, that the body first..." To conclude, it is manifest through experiment that light and darkness and odor and sound do not cause any effect in insensible bodies, unless perhaps by accident, insofar as brute bodies sometimes act by means of these qualities, as air when there is thunder splits wood, for wood suffers not from sound speaking per se, but from the air moved.

Third, at the point "but the tangibles," he shows it to be otherwise regarding tangible qualities, and he says that tangibles and humors, that is, pores, make a certain effect in sensibles, but it must be well understood regarding flavors, not insofar as it is tangible, and insofar as it is touch. If insensible bodies did not suffer from sensible qualities, it would not be to posit from what they would suffer and alter inanimate bodies, for tangibles are the active and passive qualities of the elements, from which alteration happens universally in bodies. 

Fourth, at the point "therefore, lest those," he shows also that other tangible sensibles act on certain inanimate things, but not all; he says therefore "lest those," he shows others make some effect, and smell, on inanimate things, which he says, but yet not every body is passive from odor and sound, as every body is passive from heat and cold. But from these sensibles, only indeterminate bodies can suffer, and those which do not remain, like air and water which are humid and not well determinable by their own limit, and that air can suffer from odor is manifest because the air reeks as something suffering from odor—another letter has "carries," because namely the media and other sensibles carry the species to the sense—but of such diversity it is: because tangible qualities are the causes of other sensibles, and therefore they have more of active virtue, and they can act on whatever bodies; but other sensibles which have less of active virtue cannot act except on very passive bodies, and thus also the reason is regarding the light of celestial bodies which alter inferior bodies. 

"Who, therefore," where he is, he resolves the reason and the position, saying: because if anything suffers from odor that does not smell, what is to smell except to suffer something from odor? And he answers that to smell is thus to suffer from odor and to sense the odor, and it is not thus suffering so that it senses because it does not have a sensitive power, but it is thus suffering so that it is a sensible insofar as it is a medium in the sense.

Sed jam ex tantis cruciatibus gravi quoque morbo confectus, petebat sibi dari confessorem, sperans mitius secum actum iri, quia se ritibus ipsorum accommodaret. Que spes aliquandiu illum lactavit: nam remissiore deinceps usus est custodia, in qua annum mansit, exceptis diebus septem. Interea Ioannes Hussius a tyrannis illis injuste condemnatus, comburitur octavo a feriis Petri & Pauli die. Ac circiter festum nativitatis Mariae virginis eodem anno, Hieronymum diuturnis vinculis confectum ad se evocari jusserunt, eiq[ue] multis minis propositis persuadere conati sunt, ut decederet a sententia, & condemnationi Ioannis Hussii jure, ut ajebant, combusti subscriberet. Ibi ille per infirmitatem lapsus, partim horrore supplicij, partim spe evadendi ex ipsorum crudelissimis manibus, formulam abjurationis sibi datam ex scripto publice recitavit: addidit praeterea in gratiam illorum, Hussium jure igni absumptum. Quo quidem facto non evadebat, sed ad eandem turrim deductus, minus severe quam antea tractabatur.

Jam vero sequenti anno M.CCCC.XVI. accesserunt novi hostes Carmelitae ex Bohemia, qui novas accusationes habebant adversus Hieronymum. Horum adveneu gavisi pestilentissimi nebulones Michael de causis & magister Paletz apostatae, pergunt urgere causam adversus Hieronymum, quem ipsi certis indiciis collegerant non ex animo renuntiasse suae doctrinae, sed id tantum formidine paena fecisse, atque spe liberationis: instant apud Cardinales, qui in eo Concilio judiciis praesidebant, ut reum ad crimina a prioribus diversa respondere cogant. Verum illi perspecta ini

<column-break/>

iniquitate, etsi non omnino, tamen aliquatenus remissiores, non statim ad nova illa crimina respondere cogebant, sed tempus deliberandi dabant. Quod cum viderent illi, non desinebant instare, ut Hieronymus in vinculis arctioribus teneretur, ne forte elaberetur. Quod et factum est: nam in carcerem obscurum et foetidum conjectus, catenis pedes et manus vincti sunt, ita ut movere se non posset. In hoc miserrimo statu, ubi per aliquot menses jacuisset, et fame ac squalore pene consumptus esset, tandem ad judicium productus est. Ubi cum viderent eum non esse fractum animo, sed constantem, et ad omnia paratum, rursus ad torturas et carceres redierunt, ut eum vel morte vel constantiae mutatione perderent. Sed ille, qui jam antea periculum sui fecerat, et in seipso expertus esset, quam infirma esset humana natura, cum a Deo deseritur, nunc totus in Deum conversus, et orationibus ac meditationibus intentus, omnem metum mortis excusserat, et ad certamen illud supremum, quod pro veritate Christi subiturus erat, se totum paraverat.

But now, consumed by such great tortures and also by a grave disease, he requested that a confessor be given to him, hoping that he would be dealt with more mildly because he would accommodate himself to their rites. This hope sustained him for some time, for he afterwards experienced a more relaxed custody, in which he remained for a year, except for seven days. Meanwhile, John Hus, having been unjustly condemned by those tyrants, was burned on the eighth day after the feast of Peter and Paul. And around the feast of the Nativity of the Virgin Mary in the same year, they ordered Jerome, who was worn out by long imprisonment, to be summoned to them. Having proposed many threats to him, they attempted to persuade him to depart from his opinion and to subscribe to the condemnation of John Hus, who, as they said, had been justly burned. There, having fallen through weakness, partly by the horror of the punishment and partly by the hope of escaping from their most cruel hands, he publicly recited from a writing the formula of abjuration given to him. He added, moreover, for their favor, that Hus had been justly consumed by fire. By this deed he did not escape, but was led back to the same tower, though he was treated less severely than before.

Now indeed in the following year, 1416, new enemies, Carmelites from Bohemia, arrived, who held new accusations against Jerome. The most pestilent scoundrels Michael de Causis and Master Paletz, apostates, rejoiced at their arrival and proceeded to urge the cause against Jerome. They had gathered by certain signs that he had not renounced his doctrine from the heart, but had only done so from fear of punishment and the hope of liberation. They insisted with the Cardinals, who presided over the judgments in that Council, that they should force the defendant to answer to crimes different from the previous ones. But those Cardinals, having perceived the
</column>

<column-break/>

<column>
iniquity, although not entirely, yet were to some extent more relaxed. They did not immediately force him to answer those new crimes but gave him time for deliberating. When those men saw this, they did not cease to insist that Jerome be held in tighter bonds, lest perhaps he should slip away. And this was done. For, having been cast into a dark and foul prison, his feet and hands were bound with chains so that he could not move himself. In this most miserable state, where he had lain for several months and was almost consumed by hunger and filth, he was finally brought to judgment. When they saw there that he was not broken in mind but was constant and prepared for all things, they returned again to tortures and prisons, so that they might destroy him either by death or by a change of his constancy. But he, who had already before made a trial of himself and had experienced in himself how weak human nature is when it is deserted by God, now turned entirely toward God and, intent upon prayers and meditations, had shaken off all fear of death. He had prepared himself entirely for that supreme contest which he was about to undergo for the truth of Christ.

In the middle of summer, a large infusion of cold water on a fleshy body causes the revocation of heat, but this heat then releases. In cases of pain and swelling in the joints, without wounding, and for gout and spasms, the first application of much cold water cools and attenuates, and it dissolves the pain.

<meta>A decorative initial C.</meta> At this point, I will not be silent about a matter worthy of memory, which I record not for praise or glory, but so that you may perceive that I have not been useless to your affairs, but rather worthy of honor and no small price among those men. For when your father, the illustrious Marquis Nicolaus, of memorable recollection, was vexed in no small way by gout and spasm in the joints of his right hand, to the point that he had summoned a priest and decided to commit himself into the hands of the Lord, he called me to provide care while he was languishing for many hours. And when I had tried many medicines by which he had been helped to be freed from gouty pain, they contributed nothing in any part, so that he, being completely destitute of all hope, said: "Behold, my father, I entrust my body into your hands; for I feel that I am dying, and let it not be drawn out for a long time." I replied: "If your lordship will obey my instructions, I will immediately free you from this wicked pain." And, submitting himself to my wish, I sprinkled much cold water over the joint, and it absolved him so that the pain immediately subsided, if not entirely. After a little while, he rested in sleep, and upon waking, as he felt the beginning of the pain, he cried out: "Behold, the enemy comes!" And again, with the cold water poured over the joint by the physician Franciscus, the pain was lifted. Afterward, he rested in sleep, and upon waking, he felt the beginning of the pain again, and Francischinus met it again with water. Thus, he ceased by sleep, and until twilight, during which he slept for long hours, the pain ceased entirely, and he was not troubled by it anymore thereafter.

<meta>A decorative initial B.</meta> For truly, cold waters, even if they revive heat by accident through <term>antiparistasis</term> <gloss>the intensification of one quality by the presence of its opposite</gloss>, do not operate this way in every body; for in a weak body, it is extinguished. Therefore, I advise those who are weak in heat and have fragile limbs to abstain from the cold water bath, especially in the long duration of it. Therefore, let parents take care that their children do not go to swim in such waters, for they can easily understand that they will incur putrid fevers, chronic illnesses, and evil ailments. For the heat is extinguished, thus the humors putrefy from the obstruction by which the transpiration of putrid vapors is prevented, and the members, including the principal ones, are weakened. And thus, in evil causes, there is an addition of things productive of evil ailments.

<column-break/>

Furthermore, the compound cold water shares various actions and properties, which it would be difficult to enumerate.

<meta>A decorative initial L.</meta> Limbs of the head. It harms those who have a weak brain. But to those who have a warm and strong brain, if it is cold, a light and moderate bathing of cold water, done after washing with warm lye, is perhaps suitable for those from across the Alps. For thus it thickens the skin, revokes heat, and strengthens it, and thus resolves superfluous humidities and vapors. Therefore, they are also helped with rheumatism. And the masters of steam rooms, after men have been warmed and seek to leave the steam room, pour cold water over them, taught by experience, not by reason. However, not distinguishing between the virtues of men and their figure or constitution, they often commit an error. Therefore, in those who are weak and have fragile limbs, it is more wholesome to pour the water not over them, but around them. Therefore, you, my lord, should consult your physicians carefully in this matter. For since this operation is unaccustomed among the Italians, and especially for the head, it will perhaps be disparaged by some, who, even if they yield to reasons, will perhaps turn to a contrary opinion. For which reason, that usage of our matrons is to be cultivated, who, after the washing of infants' heads, sprinkle the forehead, face, and parts of the neck with cold water, also intending to extinguish the sharpness of the lye. And the submersion of the eyes in cold water strengthens the eyes, comforting the spirits and helping toward the resolution of vapors.

<meta>A decorative initial L.</meta> Limbs of the chest.

<meta>A decorative initial N.</meta> It harms those who have a weak chest, and in them, it induces hoarseness of voice and a cough. It harms their heart and disposes them to various illnesses.

<meta>A decorative initial L.</meta> Limbs of nutrition. It harms the stomach severely, especially if it is cold and weak. But it strengthens a strong and well-disposed one, fortifies digestion, excites the appetite for food, and by sharpening the bile, it lubricates the belly. It excites pain of the intestines, inducing tenesmus. It offends weak and cold kidneys, and in coitus, it provides weakness, and it harms the womb. Truly, in the flow of red, choleric menstrual blood, a bath of cold water works miraculously in their retention, as some experts prescribe for women to sit in it thus.

<meta>A decorative initial L.</meta> Limbs of the joints.

<meta>A decorative initial N.</meta> It harms the nerves and joints by itself, and especially the weak ones, even if sometimes it is helped by it by accident, as has been acted upon.

<meta>A decorative initial N.</meta> Wounds and ulcers.

<meta>A decorative initial N.</meta> It harms wounds and ulcers with its coldness. Whence, 22.5, cold and biting to ulcers induces skin...

<margin>lentinſque converſo</margin> 114 Confonat hic quidem Synchronus noſter cum ante dictis, in quina apparitione, ab ipſo met Raymundo expreſſa. <margin>quod ipſi-met confessionis magis jonat.</margin> B Non eo hæc dicta ſunt, ut ſpiranti divinæ gratiæ metas ſtatuamus aut terminos, [quæ ſolo fatu, ut recte notat de Pax, de citharœdo Propheta, de Pifcatore prædicatorem, Doctorem de perſecutore, de publicano fecit Euangeliftam; cujus præſentiſſimus ignis, nullas ad mutandum humana corda moras expectat.] Non hæc, inquam, in diſputationem adducimus, qui ſolis Auctorum antilogiis concordandis hic inſudamus. His porro expediendis uſui eſſe exiſtimo quod inſinuaveruperius, Synchronum nempe, tametſi in re ipſa ab aliis diſcrepet, primordia nihilominus Lullianæ converſionis, minus ex ordine digeſſiſſe, ea confuſe narrando, quæ reliqui paulo accuratius diſtinxere. Nifi quis malat, Bovillo & de Pax, tamquam recentioribus neglectis, ſoli Anonymo ſubſcribendum, in quo nihil magnopere, ad ceteras Raymundi actiones ordinate pertexendas, accidere poteſt detrimenti. Fortaffis autem ſic poterant ambo illi, cum Anonymo conciliari; ſi concipiatur Raymundus, conſpectu exulcerati pectoris inductus ad agnitionem cordiæ ſuæ; necdum tamen converſus ad Dei unius amorem; in eoque affectionum conflictu, exorſus eſſe poëma, utrique ſubſerviens paſſioni, quod Anonymus Amatariam cantilenam dicere potuerit, qualibus ſcilicet antea aſsueverat; alii maluerint Flebile carmen nominare: de quo, donec in lucem proeat, liberum fit in alterutram partem judicare. Statue igitur proinde, Lector, ut lubet, dum nos interim ad alia gradum facimus.

<margin>Addunt alii apparitionem Deipare, à Coevo quidem præteritam.</margin> 115 Prædictis Crucifixi apparitionibus memorabilem aliam ſubjungunt ſcriptores quamplurimi, cujus tamen Auctores noſtri non meminere; quamque proinde ſilentio præteriiſſem, niſi Raymundus ipſe illius fidem faceret prope indubitatam. Narrat Vincentius Mut, Virginem Deiparam, infantem brachiis geſtantem, Raymundo ſe exhibuiſſe ad portam Almudai, vicinam horto palatii Epifcopalis; in cujus perpetuam memoriam imago illic collocata fuerit; quæ uſque hodie, inquit, eo loci conſpicitur: mutata eſt poſtmodum, uti teſtatur Culturerius. His affinia tradit Vernonus & alii paſſim; quorum omnium ſuffragiis nihil prorfus tribuerem, niſi me ejuſmet Beati moveret teſtimonium, ita in Blaquer-

Quapropter nobis placet, inquit Rex, quod ipſe ab omnibus orthodoxæ fidei cultoribus, & præcipue ſubditis noſtris tractetur perbenigniter, ipſique favor benevolus impendatur, quem gratum habemus & acceptum. Upon seeing this from the cross, he was afraid, and leaving what he had in his hands, he entered his bed to sleep. But rising on the morrow and returning to his usual vanities, he did not care about that vision. Indeed, as soon as eight days later, in the same place as before and at the same hour, he again prepared himself to write and finish his aforesaid song, to whom the Lord again appeared on the cross as before. He then, terrified more than the first time, entered his bed again and, as before, fell asleep. But still on the morrow, neglecting the appearance made to him, he did not leave his lewdness. Indeed, after a little while, he strove to finish the song he had begun, until the Savior appeared to him a third and a fourth time successively, with some days coming between, always in the same form as the first, etc.

<margin>and to one slowly converted</margin> 114 Here our contemporary author agrees with those mentioned before regarding the five appearances expressed by Raymond himself. But indeed, that which I was saying just now is now clear: it is perhaps less likely that a man occupied in writing obscene verses would have felt those favors, which others more appropriately judged should be attributed to a repenting Raymond agitated by the stings of conscience.

<margin>which sounds more like his own confession.</margin> B These things are not said so that we may set boundaries or limits to breathing divine grace, [which by a single breath, as de Pax rightly notes, made a Prophet out of a harp-player, a preacher out of a Fisherman, a Doctor out of a persecutor, and an Evangelist out of a publican; whose most present fire waits for no delays to change human hearts.] We do not, I say, bring these things into dispute, we who labor here only to reconcile the contradictions of the Authors. Furthermore, to resolve these matters, I think it useful what I suggested earlier: namely, that the contemporary author, although he differs from others in the matter itself, nevertheless arranged the beginnings of Lull's conversion with less order, narrating confusedly those things which the rest distinguished a little more accurately. Unless one prefers that Bovillus and de Pax, being more recent, should be neglected, and only the Anonymous author should be followed, in which case nothing can happen that greatly harms the orderly weaving together of Raymond's other actions. But perhaps both of those could be reconciled with the Anonymous author if it is conceived that Raymond, induced by the sight of the ulcerated breast to recognize his own misery, but not yet converted to the love of God alone, began in that conflict of affections a poem serving both passions. This the Anonymous author could call a "Love Song," of the kind he was previously accustomed to, while others preferred to name it a "Mournful Song." Concerning this, until it comes to light, one is free to judge in either direction. Therefore, Reader, decide as you please, while we meanwhile step toward other things.

<margin>Others add an appearance of the Mother of God, omitted indeed by the contemporary.</margin> 115 To the aforesaid appearances of the Crucified One, many writers subjoin another memorable one, which our authors nonetheless did not mention, and which I would have passed over in silence unless Raymond himself made its truth nearly beyond doubt. Vicente Mut relates that the Virgin Mother of God, carrying the infant in her arms, showed herself to Raymond at the gate of Almudaina, near the garden of the Episcopal palace. In perpetual memory of this, an image was placed there, which he says is seen in that place to this day; it was later changed, as Culturerius witnesses. Vernonus and others here and there pass down similar things. I would give nothing at all to the votes of all these, unless the testimony of the Blessed man himself moved me, writing thus in *Blanquerna* <note>a famous novel by Lull</note> number 14 of the Paris edition of 1632 which I have at hand. [The Queen of Heaven presented her son to her friend so that he might kiss his feet, and so that he might write the praises and virtues of the Mother of his Beloved in his book.] Furthermore, it is more certain that Raymond is understood by the "friend" than can come into dispute. That which was prescribed, he diligently performed here in the book *On the Praises of the Most Blessed Virgin*, published at Paris by Jean Petit in 1499.

<margin>D</margin>
<margin>sufficiently certain by the testimony of that Saint.</margin>

116 I will briefly explain here what our authors report everywhere concerning the approval of Raymond's doctrine by the Academy of Paris, and others obtained from King Philip and from the Chancellor of the University. I said in section 7, number 76, that the Lullian Art was subjected to the examination of forty Parisian theologians in 1309. Culturerius produces the instrument on page 206: [Furthermore, the said Masters were present... by their oaths before our aforesaid sworn officials, that the said Art or Science was good, useful, necessary... and that there was nothing in it against the Catholic faith,] but much for the maintenance of said faith. King Philip makes it known that [having heard Master Raymond Lull, he considers him from his present character to be a good, just, and Catholic man, faithfully insisting on the confirmation and exaltation of the Catholic faith. Therefore it pleases us, says the King, that he be treated most kindly by all worshippers of the orthodox faith, and especially our subjects, and that benevolent favor be bestowed upon him, which we hold as pleasing and accepted. In testimony of which thing, we have caused our seal to be applied to the present letters; Given at Vernon on August 11, 1310.] Nicolaus de Pax reads "Verona." Whichever you prefer, it makes no difference: both are cities in France, this one in Maine, that one situated in Normandy. Finally, Francis of Naples left a testament in 1311, [that he found nothing in them which opposes good morals and is adverse to sacred theological doctrine.] You may see the rest in Culturerius, pages 207, 528, and 531; where you will also find resolved whether the famous Scotus <note>Duns Scotus</note> is to be named among Lull's approvers. Furthermore, the things that pertain to the Blessed man’s entire doctrine, we have pushed back to the end of this Treatise; let these few things suffice to save the credibility of the Acts.

<margin>E</margin>
<margin>from King Philip</margin>

Section X. Concerning the florins assigned by King James for endowing the College of Languages which Lull founded; and concerning the mastic leaves inscribed with letters on Mount Randa.

117 There is also a doubt to be elucidated regarding the foundation of the monastery for learning languages made by the King of Majorca around the year 1276, as I said in section 6, number 60. A difficulty could turn on the fact that in the Acts written by some contemporary of Raymond, chapter 2, number 13, five hundred florins are said to be provided annually for the needs of those Religious men. It is certain enough that that monastery, although erected by Pontifical authority, later fell into ruin by I know not whose fault. The question is whether the currency of florins was known to the Majorcans at that time. Otherwise, some more austere Critic could immediately suspect that that life of Raymond is later than his time, and therefore to be reduced only to those times in which florins began to be known in that kingdom. I remained uncertain about what to decide on this.

<margin>F</margin>
<margin>He doubts whether this currency was used in Majorca</margin>

Ideoque subjeci estote, non tantum propter iram, sed & propter conscientiam. Propter hoc enim & tributa penditis: ministri enim Dei sunt in hoc ipsum fervientes. Sed & Dominus igitur & Apostoli unum Deum Patrem annuntiant eum, qui legiſlationem fecit, qui misit Prophetas, qui omnia fecit: & propter hoc ait: Mittens exercitus suos: quoniam omnis homo, secundum quod Dei suum, plasma ipsius est, licet ignoret Deum suum. Omnibus enim ut ſint præstat, qui solem suum oriri facit super malos & bonos, & pluit super justos & injustos.

7. Et non solum per ea quæ prædicta sunt, ſed & per parabolam duorum filiorum, quorum minor luxurioſe consumsit substantiam, vivens cum fornicariis, unum & eumdem docuit Patrem, majori quidem filio ne hædum quidem indulgentem; propter eum autem qui perierat, minoremque filium suum, jubentem occidi vitulum saginatum, & primam ei stolam donantem.

Et per parabolam autem eorum operariorum, qui variis temporibus in vineam mittebantur, unus & idem Dominus ostenditur: vocans alios quidem statim in initio mundi fabricationis; alios vero post hoc; & alios circa medietatem temporum; & alios progredſis jam temporibus & item alios in fine: ut sint quidem multi operarii secundum sua ipsorum tempora, unus autem qui convocat eos, paterfamilias. Etenim vinea una, quoniam & una justitia: & unus dispensator; unus enim Spiritus Dei, qui disponit omnia: similiter autem & merces una; omnes enim acciperunt singulos denarios, imaginem & inscriptionem Regis, & agnitionem Filii Dei quæ est incorrupta. Et propter hoc a novissimis cœpit dare mercedem, quoniam in novissimis temporibus manifestatus Dominus, omnibus semetipsum repræsentavit.
