For just as in the former Testament He did not find favor with many of them, so it is also here: many are called, but few are chosen. It is not one God who judges and another Father who calls us to salvation. It is not one who grants eternal light and another who orders those without a wedding garment to be cast into the outer darkness. Instead, He is one and the same Lord, the Father of our Lord, by whom the Prophets were also sent. In His immense kindness, He calls those who are unworthy, but He examines those who have been called to see if they have a garment that is suitable and fitting for the wedding of His Son, because nothing unfitting or evil is pleasing to Him. As the Lord said to the man who had been healed: Behold, you have been made well; sin no more, lest something worse happen to you. For He who is good, just, pure, and spotless will not tolerate anything evil, unjust, or abominable in His wedding chamber. This is the Father of our Lord, by whose providence all things consist, and by whose command all things are administered. He gives freely to those whom it is proper to give, but as a most just rewarder, He distributes according to merit most worthily against those who are ungrateful and do not perceive His kindness. And for this reason He says: Sending His armies, He destroyed those murderers and burned their city. He calls them "His army" because all men belong to God. For the earth is the Lord's, and its fullness, the world, and all who dwell in it. For this reason, the Apostle Paul says in the epistle to the Romans: For there is no power except from God. But those that exist have been ordained by God. Therefore, whoever resists the power resists the ordinance of God, and those who resist bring damnation upon themselves. For rulers are not a terror to good work, but to evil. Do you wish not to fear the power? Do good, and you will have praise from it, for he is God’s servant to you for good. But if you do evil, be afraid. For he does not carry the sword without cause. He is God’s servant, an avenger for wrath against him who does evil. Therefore, be subject, not only because of wrath, but also because of conscience. For this reason you also pay taxes, for they are God’s ministers serving for this very purpose. Thus, both the Lord and the Apostles announce one God the Father, the one who made the legislation, who sent the Prophets, and who made all things. Because of this, He says: Sending His armies; for every human being, insofar as he is God’s own, is His handiwork, even if he is ignorant of his God. For He grants existence to all, making His sun to rise over the evil and the good, and raining upon the just and the unjust.

7. This is taught not only through the things previously mentioned, but also through the parable of the two sons. The younger son luxuriously consumed his substance, living with prostitutes. He showed that there is one and the same Father, who did not even grant a young goat to the elder son, but for the sake of the one who had been lost, His younger son, He ordered the fatted calf to be killed and gave him the best robe.

And through the parable of those workers who were sent into the vineyard at different times, one and the same Lord is shown. He calls some immediately at the beginning of the world's creation; others after this; others around the middle of time; others as time had already progressed; and others at the end. Thus, there are many workers according to their own times, but only one householder who calls them together. For there is one vineyard, since there is also one righteousness. There is one steward, for there is one Spirit of God who arranges all things. Similarly, there is one reward, for all received a single <term>denarius</term> <gloss>a silver coin representing a day's wage</gloss>, bearing the image and inscription of the King, which is the knowledge of the Son of God, which is incorruptible. And for this reason He began to give the reward from the last ones, because the Lord, being manifested in the last times, represented Himself to all.

When infants, however, fall into such a state without atrophy <term>atrophia</term> <gloss>wasting away</gloss> that, having lost all their flesh, they barely cling to their bones, it is certain that an obstruction of the vessels is present. In Westphalia and Dithmarschen, which are close to Denmark, this disease is seen as <term>endymō</term> <gloss>a local term for a wasting condition</gloss>, which they themselves call "Varum." Our people call it the **Mitteſſer**, **Riekuchen**, or the **running and consuming worm**, named after the natural action that is damaged and the aforementioned symptoms. Old toothless women, under the holy pretext of religion, apply various exorcisms, various incantations, and various gesticulations with the patient’s belt. Furthermore, they smear the area with wheat flour worked with honey and expose it to the heat of a furnace or a dry bath so that a large crowd of little worms, in the form of living ascarids <term>askaridōn</term> <gloss>pinworms</gloss>, crawl out from the pores, which are then scraped away with a razor. But since this method of operating not only disappoints most people but is partly worthy of fire and partly of laughter, it is better, once the body has been gently evacuated, to give a powder of earthworms with oxysaccharum <term>acidic sugar syrup</term> or theriac in milk or chicken broth, or the juice of turnips with sugar candy, or the electuary of roses with rhubarb. Then let the child be placed in a bath of fresh water prepared from the ashes of hazel trees and goat’s milk. Finally, after the bath, rub the limbs and joints with oil of almonds or an ointment of marjoram, nightshade, and butter. Furthermore, to dislodge the worms, in addition to the above, let a few grains of the following powder be given in a distilled liquor of grass. Take of stag horn, coral, of each 0.5 dram, rhubarb 12 grains; let them be mixed to make a very fine powder. At the same time, let the pulse of the arms, the mouth of the stomach, the navel, and the entire abdomen down to the groin be anointed with that viscous and foul-smelling fat which exudes from the bladder of a wild boar, if this is suspended in the shade in a moment, having extracted the dart, unharmed with the urine. Finally, in a cough, give the electuary <term>Dia botyros</term> <gloss>a buttery electuary</gloss> and oil of sweet almonds recently extracted with sugar candy (with which the chest and the palms of the feet can also be anointed over coals), or give honey of violets to be licked, or goat’s milk just milked with water of fennel or coltsfoot.

Dionysius, *Divine Names*, chapter 13: that there is no multitude not participating in the 'one': but those that are many in parts are one in a whole: and those that are many in accidents are one in subject: those that are many in number are one in species: those that are many in species are one in genus: those that are many in processes are one in principle. To the third it is said: therefore it is not a redundancy when one says 'being one': because 'one' adds according to reason over being.

Second article: Whether 'one' and 'many' are opposed.
To the second, it is proceeded thus: it seems that 'one' and 'many' are not opposed. No opposite is predicated of its opposite: but every multitude is in a certain way one: as appears from the aforesaid: that 'one' is not opposed to multitude. Furthermore, no opposite is constituted from its opposite: but 'one' constitutes multitude: therefore it is not opposed to multitude. Furthermore, 'one' is an opposite: but 'many' is opposed to 'few': therefore 'one' is not opposed to it. Furthermore, if 'one' is opposed to multitude: it is as the undivided is to the divided: and thus it will be opposed to it as a privation to a habit: this, however, is inconvenient: because it follows that 'one' is posterior to multitude: and is defined by it: since multitude is defined by 'one'. There would be a circle in the definition: which is inconvenient: therefore 'one' and 'many' are not opposed. Contra, where reasons are opposed: they themselves are opposed: but the reason of 'one' consists in indivisibility: the reason of multitude sustains division: therefore 'one' and 'many' are opposed. It must be said that 'one' is opposed to 'many' in different ways: for the 'one' that is the principle of number is opposed to multitude: which is number: as measure to the measured: for 'one' has the reason of the first measure, *Metaphysics*, book 10. The 'one' that converts with being is opposed to multitude by way of privation: as the undivided to the divided. To the first, it is said that no privation totally takes away being: for privation is a negation in a subject, according to the philosopher <note>Aristotle</note>. Yet every privation takes away some [perfection]: and therefore in being, by reason of its commonality, it happens that the privation of being is founded in being: which does not happen in the privations of spiritual forms such as sight or whiteness or others: there [it is different]: and as it is with being: so it is with 'one' and 'good': and similarly the removal of unity is founded in some 'one': and consequently it happens that multitude is a certain 'one': and evil is a certain 'good': and 'not-being' is a certain 'being': not, however, opposed in every way. In act: or that which is simply in the genus of substance: is 'not-being' in a certain respect, which is some accidental being. Conversely: and similarly, that which is 'one' simply is 'evil' simply or heterogeneous: which is composed of dissimilar parts: a certain good of the whole: just as every part of water is water: and such is the constitution [of that which is] constituted from its parts. In every heterogeneous whole, however, every part lacks the form of the whole. For no part of a house is a house: nor is any part of a man a man: and such a whole is a multitude, insofar as its part does not have the form of the multitude, the multitude is composed of units: just as a house [is composed] of houses: not that the units constitute the multitude according to that which they have by reason of indivision: as they are opposed to multitude: but according to this, that they are certain bodies: not because they are not houses. To the third, it is said that 'many' is accepted in two ways. One, absolutely, and thus it is opposed to 'one'. The other, according to which it implies a certain excess: and thus it is opposed to 'few'. One, first, two are many: not, however, in the second [way].

To the fourth, it is said that 'one' is opposed to the privation of 'many' insofar as in the reason of 'many' it is that they are divided. It is said that division is made before unity, not simply, but according to the reason of our apprehension. For we apprehend simple things through composed things. *Metaphysics*, book 7: we define a point, of which there is no part, as the principle of a line: but multitude also according to reason follows 'one': because we do not understand the divided to have the reason of multitude: except by the fact that we attribute unity to both of the divided [parts]. Whence 'one' is put in the definition of multitude: not, however, is multitude put in the definition of 'one': but division falls into the intellect from the very negation of being: so that first 'being' falls into the intellect. Second, that this being is not that being: and thus we secondarily apprehend division: third, 'one': fourth, multitude.

<column-break/>

Third article: Whether God is one.
To the third, it is proceeded thus: it seems that God is not one. It is said, 1 Corinthians 8: "For there be gods many, and lords many." Furthermore, 'one' which is the principle of number cannot be predicated of God: since no quantity is predicated of God: similarly, nor 'one' which converts with being: which imports privation: and every privation is an imperfection: which does not suit God. Therefore it is not true that God is one. But against this is what is said, Deuteronomy 6: "Hear, O Israel, thy God is one." It must be said that God is one is demonstrated from three [points]. First, from his simplicity. It is manifest that that 'one' is some singular [thing], this something: not in any way communicable to a multitude. That which is 'one' in form is good: it can be communicated to many: but that which is 'one' in being cannot be communicated except to one term: if this were a man, he would be a man by that which he is this man: just as there cannot be many strengths: so there could not be many men: but this pertains to God. For God himself is one nature, as was shown in the first question, article three. Therefore, since he is one and the same [in nature], it is impossible that there be many gods. Second, from the infinity of his perfection: as shown in the first question, article four, that God comprehends in himself all perfection. If there were many gods, it would be necessary that they differ in something that would belong to one and not to another: and thus that one would have a privation, and thus would not be simply perfect: but if this is the supreme perfection: one must posit one only. Third, from the unity of the world. Things are found to be ordered to one another: for some are defined by others: those that are diverse would not arrive in one order, unless they were ordered by some one [thing]. For it is better that many be reduced into one order by one than by many: because the cause of one [effect] is one by itself: and many are not the cause of one except by accident: insofar as the common [good] is made most perfect and by itself, not by accident: it is necessary that the first [principle] reducing all into one order be one only: and this is God. To the first, it must be said that they say 'many gods' according to the error of some: who worshipped many gods, thinking that the planets and other stars were gods: or also individual [things].

Because when they are molded from these kinds, first they become heavy; then, when they are sprinkled by rain on the walls, they slip away and dissolve; and the straw that is put into them does not hold together because of the roughness. They must be made from white, chalky earth, or from red ochre, or even from coarse sand. For these kinds possess firmness because of their lightness, and they are not heavy in the work, and they are gathered more easily. They are to be molded during the spring and autumn time so that they may dry out evenly. Those that are prepared during the solstice are defective for this reason: when the sun harshly bakes the top skin, it makes them appear dry, but inside they are not dry; and when they subsequently contract while drying, they break through the parts that were dry, and thus, having become cracked, they are made weak. They will be most useful if they have been molded two years before, for they cannot dry out thoroughly before then. Therefore, when fresh and undried ones are built into a structure, and the plaster is applied and it remains rigidly hardened, the bricks themselves—shrinking—cannot maintain the same height as the plaster; moved by contraction, they do not adhere to it, but are separated from its connection. Therefore, the plasters, detached from the structure, cannot stand by themselves because of their thinness, but are broken, and the walls themselves, shrinking by chance, are spoiled. Therefore, even the Viticenses, if a brick is dry and was molded five years before, when it has been approved at the discretion of the magistrate, then they use it in the structure of walls.

There are three kinds of bricks. One, which is called in Greek πλίνθιον brick/tile—that is, the one we use—is a foot long and half a foot wide. Greek buildings are constructed with the other two. Of these, one is called pentadoron, the other tetradoron. The Greeks call a palm a doron, because the giving of gifts is called δῶρον in Greek; this is always handled by the palm of the hand. OF MEDICINES FROM <term>PARTHENIUM</term>. CHAPTER XXX.

Some call <term>parthenium</term> <gloss>feverfew</gloss> by the name <term>leucanthemum</term>, others <term>thanacum</term>. Celsus, in our language, calls it <term>pellecium</term> and <term>muralium</term>. It grows in gardens and hedges, with a white flower, an apple-like scent, and a bitter taste. It is used as a decoction for hardness of the womb and for inflammations. Dried and applied with honey and vinegar, it draws out black bile. For this reason, it is useful against dizziness and for those with kidney stones. It is also applied to holy fire <gloss>erysipelas</gloss>. Likewise for scrofula when mixed with old lard. Magicians order that it be plucked with the left hand against tertian fevers, that one should say whose name it is being plucked for, and that one should not look back. Then, they place a leaf of it under the tongue of the patient so that it may soon be swallowed in a cup of water.

OF MEDICINES FROM <term>STRYCHNE</term>. CHAPTER XXXI.

Would that they did not use <term>strychne</term> <gloss>nightshade</gloss>—which some have written as <term>strychnum</term>—for wreaths in Egypt, as the similarity of its leaves to ivy misleads them. It has two kinds: one has scarlet berries in granular pods. They call it <term>halicaccabum</term> and <term>halicallion</term>; our people call it <term>vesicaria</term> <gloss>bladder-herb</gloss>, because it is beneficial for sheep and kidney stones. It is a branched shrub, or rather an herb, with large, wide, and conical pods; it is known by the berry which it produces in the month of November. The leaves of the third kind are like those of basil and must be demonstrated carefully. For these remedies are not to be taken lightly, since the juice alone induces insanity, which the Greek authors have even mentioned in jest. They say that a weight of a drachm induces a sense of shame, demonstrating that one observes vain hopes and conspicuous images. It doubles this way: it induces legitimate insanity. Truly, whatever is added to the weight results in death. This was used by those who touched the tips of their weapons in battle, so that they might be born anew, as they previously envisioned. The magicians knew things that they did not hide from others, such as <term>erythro</term> or <term>neurita</term>, as some, like Piso, have learned more carefully. For there is another kind, which they call <term>halicaccabum</term>, which is soporific and faster to death than opium; some call it <term>morio</term>, others <term>moly</term>. It was praised by Locrus to Euedus and Timaristos, who also used it in an ointment to induce forgetfulness, for it is a preferred remedy to calm those who are restless if they wash with it. To <term>halicaccabum</term> alone they added an exception: that it not be done for too long, as delirium is born from it. Nor should remedies be demonstrated whose medicine brings the danger of a greater evil. For it is eaten in foods, even if it is preferred for its garden-like flavors. And there is nothing among the evils of the body for which <term>strychnos</term> is not healthy, as Xenocrates proclaims. However, their aids are not so great that it would be considered a sacrilege not to mention them, especially given such an abundance of harmless medicines. They drink the root of <term>halicaccabum</term> when those who are skilled in prophecy wish to be seen as mad in order to confirm their predictions. It is a remedy; I would rather report it as having been given in copious warm honey-wine. Nor will I omit that it kills by the power of sleep. Therefore, crushed in oil, it helps those who have been struck.

OF <term>CORCORUS</term>. CHAPTER XXXII.

<term>Corcorus</term> <gloss>jew’s mallow</gloss> is an herb of the Alexandrians, with curled leaves similar to those of the mulberry. It is useful for the midriff, and for hair loss and lichen <gloss>a skin condition</gloss>. It is also used to treat the mange of cattle very quickly, according to Nicander, and it is used for the bites of serpents before they flower. Nor shall I argue at length about <term>cnicus</term> or <term>atractylis</term>. It is an Egyptian herb and provides great aid against venomous animals. Likewise against fungi. It is agreed that those struck by a scorpion do not feel the torture as long as they hold that herb. 

OF <term>PFOLUTA</term>. CHAPTER XXXIII.

Egypt sows <term>pfoluta</term> in gardens for wreaths; there are two kinds: female and male. Both are highly reported to inhibit men's desire when taken. 

OF MEASURES AND WEIGHTS. CHAPTER XXXIV.

And since one must frequently use Greek terms for measures and weights, I will place their interpretation here once. The Attic drachma—for doctors use the Attic observation—has the weight of a silver denarius. It makes six obols in weight. An obol is ten chalchi. A cyathus weighs ten drachms by itself. When the measure of an acetabulum is spoken of, it signifies a fourth part of a hemina, that is, fifteen drachms. What our people call a mina weighs one hundred Attic drachms.
